Prior work has identified key ethical principles such as transparency, fairness, and accountability, and has explored the alignment between these principles and the needs of industry practitioners. However, gaps remain in how these principles can be systematically integrated into the development and deployment of machine learning systems. To address this, the work develops a structured approach that maps ethical considerations to specific stages of the machine learning pipeline, enabling developers to apply ethical reasoning in practice. It evaluates the feasibility of this approach through case studies and analysis of existing tools, assessing how well they support the implementation of ethical principles in real-world scenarios. The findings highlight opportunities for refining both technical methods and the frameworks that guide their application.

original_abstract: This paper develops several average-case reduction techniques to show new hardness results for three central high-dimensional statistics problems, implying a statistical-computational gap induced by robustness, a detection-recovery gap and a universality principle for these gaps. A main feature of our approach is to map to these problems via a common intermediate problem that we introduce, which we call Imbalanced Sparse Gaussian Mixtures. We assume the planted clique conjecture for a version of the planted clique problem where the position of the planted clique is mildly constrained, and from this obtain the following computational lower bounds: (1) a $k$-to-$k^2$ statistical-computational gap for robust sparse mean estimation, providing the first average-case evidence for a conjecture of Li (2017) and Balakrishnan et al. (2017); (2) a tight lower bound for semirandom planted dense subgraph, which shows that a semirandom adversary shifts the detection threshold in planted dense subgraph to the conjectured recovery threshold; and (3) a universality principle for $k$-to-$k^2$ gaps in a broad class of sparse mixture problems that includes many natural formulations such as the spiked covariance model. #R##N#Our main approach is to introduce several average-case techniques to produce structured and Gaussianized versions of an input graph problem, and then to rotate these high-dimensional Gaussians by matrices carefully constructed from hyperplanes in $\mathbb{F}_r^t$. For our universality result, we introduce a new method to perform an algorithmic change of measure tailored to sparse mixtures. We also provide evidence that the mild promise in our variant of planted clique does not change the complexity of the problem.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of detecting structured signals in high-dimensional noisy data, where the computational efficiency of algorithms often lags behind their statistical potential. Prior work has established that many problems, such as planted clique, sparse PCA, and submatrix localization, exhibit a statistical-computational gap: while information-theoretically feasible detection is possible with sufficient data, no known polynomial-time algorithm can achieve this threshold under certain assumptions. To bridge this gap, we develop a general framework for analyzing computational barriers through average-case reductions, leveraging the planted clique conjecture as a foundation. Our approach identifies the precise conditions under which polynomial-time algorithms fail to achieve optimal detection, and we demonstrate that these limitations are not unique to specific models but are instead universal across a broad class of structured signal detection problems. We evaluate the effectiveness of our framework by applying it to several canonical models, showing that the computational barriers are tightly linked to the statistical properties of the underlying distributions. Our results provide a unified perspective on the tradeoffs between statistical accuracy and computational feasibility in high-dimensional inference.

original_abstract: The desire to map neural networks to varying-capacity devices has led to the development of a wealth of compression techniques, many of which involve replacing standard convolutional blocks in a large network with cheap alternative blocks. However, not all blocks are created equally; for a required compute budget there may exist a potent combination of many different cheap blocks, though exhaustively searching for such a combination is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we develop BlockSwap: a fast algorithm for choosing networks with interleaved block types by passing a single minibatch of training data through randomly initialised networks and gauging their Fisher potential. These networks can then be used as students and distilled with the original large network as a teacher. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the chosen networks across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet for classification, and COCO for detection, and provide a comprehensive ablation study of our approach. BlockSwap quickly explores possible block configurations using a simple architecture ranking system, yielding highly competitive networks in orders of magnitude less time than most architecture search techniques (e.g. under 5 minutes on a single GPU for CIFAR-10). Code is available at https://github.com/BayesWatch/pytorch-blockswap.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of reducing the computational and memory demands of deep neural networks while maintaining their performance. Prior work has established that significant parameter redundancy exists in trained models, enabling substantial compression through pruning, architectural redesign, and efficient training strategies. However, the optimal balance between model efficiency and performance remains an open question, particularly when considering diverse network structures and training regimes. To address this, we develop a method that integrates parameter pruning with a novel training strategy that dynamically allocates computational resources based on gradient significance. By focusing updates on the most influential weights and regenerating the rest on demand, our approach minimizes memory usage without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate the effectiveness of this method across multiple architectures and datasets, demonstrating significant reductions in parameter count and memory access while preserving state-of-the-art performance.

original_abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of generating a set ofrealistic and diverse backgrounds when given only a smallforeground region. We refer to this task as image outpaint-ing. The technical challenge of this task is to synthesize notonly plausible but also diverse image outputs. Traditionalgenerative adversarial networks suffer from mode collapse.While recent approaches propose to maximize orpreserve the pairwise distance between generated sampleswith respect to their latent distance, they do not explicitlyprevent the diverse samples of different conditional inputsfrom collapsing. Therefore, we propose a new regulariza-tion method to encourage diverse sampling in conditionalsynthesis. In addition, we propose a feature pyramid dis-criminator to improve the image quality. Our experimen-tal results show that our model can produce more diverseimages without sacrificing visual quality compared to state-of-the-arts approaches in both the CelebA face dataset and the Cityscape scene dataset.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of generating realistic and semantically coherent visual content in complex scenes, particularly when dealing with missing or incomplete information. Prior work has established methods for learning visual features through context-based prediction, adversarial training, and probabilistic modeling, which have enabled progress in tasks such as image inpainting, future frame synthesis, and text-to-image generation. However, these approaches often struggle with maintaining structural consistency, capturing high-level semantics, or generating diverse outputs that align with the input context. To address these limitations, we develop a novel framework that integrates contextual awareness, adversarial learning, and probabilistic reasoning to synthesize missing content while preserving scene coherence. Our approach employs a multi-stage model that first infers the structure of missing regions using contextual cues and then refines the output through adversarial training to ensure visual realism. We evaluate our method on a range of tasks, including semantic inpainting, image completion, and scene synthesis, demonstrating its ability to produce high-quality results that align with the input context and maintain semantic consistency.

original_abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) is one of the best methods for understanding the differences in semantic rules between two languages. Especially for Indo-European languages, subword-level models have achieved impressive results. However, when the translation task involves Chinese, semantic granularity remains at the word and character level, so there is still need more fine-grained translation model of Chinese. In this paper, we introduce a simple and effective method for Chinese translation at the sub-character level. Our approach uses the Wubi method to translate Chinese into English; byte-pair encoding (BPE) is then applied. Our method for Chinese-English translation eliminates the need for a complicated word segmentation algorithm during preprocessing. Furthermore, our method allows for sub-character-level neural translation based on recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture, without preprocessing. The empirical results show that for Chinese-English translation tasks, our sub-character-level model has a comparable BLEU score to the subword model, despite having a much smaller vocabulary. Additionally, the small vocabulary is highly advantageous for NMT model compression.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving robust and flexible neural machine translation in the presence of rare and unseen words, particularly in morphologically rich and structurally diverse languages. Prior work has established that traditional word-level models struggle with open-vocabulary translation, often relying on dictionary-based fallbacks or fixed vocabularies that limit performance. More recent approaches have explored subword and character-level modeling to better handle such cases, yet these methods often come with trade-offs in efficiency or accuracy. This work introduces a novel mechanism that combines the strengths of word-level and character-level representations, enabling the model to handle both common and rare words without explicit segmentation. The approach leverages hybrid architectures that primarily operate at the word level but dynamically consult character-based components when encountering rare or unknown words. This design allows for more efficient training and inference while maintaining the ability to generate valid target words. The model is evaluated on a range of translation tasks, demonstrating improvements in handling rare words and overall translation quality compared to existing methods.

original_abstract: While cutting-edge image captioning systems are increasingly describing an image coherently and exactly, recent progresses in continual learning allow deep learning systems to avoid catastrophic forgetting. However, the domain where image captioning working with continual learning is not exploited yet. We define the task in which we consolidate continual learning and image captioning as continual image captioning. In this work, we propose ContCap, a framework continually generating captions over a series of new tasks coming, seamlessly integrating continual learning into image captioning accompanied by tackling catastrophic forgetting. After proving catastrophic forgetting in image captioning, we employ freezing, knowledge distillation, and pseudo-labeling techniques to overcome the forgetting dilemma with the baseline is a simple fine-tuning scheme. We split MS-COCO 2014 dataset to perform experiments on incremental tasks without revisiting dataset of previously provided tasks. The experiments are designed to increase the degree of catastrophic forgetting and appraise the capacity of approaches. Experimental results show remarkable improvements in the performance on the old tasks, while the figure for the new task remains almost the same compared to fine-tuning. For example, pseudo-labeling increases CIDEr from 0.287 to 0.576 on the old task and 0.686 down to 0.657 BLEU1 on the new task.
generated_abstract: This work addresses the challenge of enabling machine learning models to incrementally acquire new knowledge without forgetting previously learned information. Prior research has established that models trained on sequential tasks often suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where performance on earlier tasks degrades when new tasks are introduced. These studies have explored various strategies, including architectural modifications, regularization techniques, and the use of memory replay, to mitigate this issue. However, open challenges remain in effectively balancing the learning of new tasks with the retention of old knowledge, particularly in scenarios where access to prior data is limited. To address this, we propose a method that leverages a carefully designed loss function to balance the learning of new classes with the preservation of knowledge from previous ones. This is achieved by incorporating a distillation component that minimizes the discrepancy between the outputs of the current and previous models for the old classes, while simultaneously learning the new classes through cross-entropy loss. The approach is evaluated on standard image classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining performance on previously learned tasks while successfully adapting to new ones.

original_abstract: Recent advancements in machine learning research, i.e., deep learning, introduced methods that excel conventional algorithms as well as humans in several complex tasks, ranging from detection of objects in images and speech recognition to playing difficult strategic games. However, the current methodology of machine learning research and consequently, implementations of the real-world applications of such algorithms, seems to have a recurring HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) issue. In this work, we elaborate on the algorithmic, economic and social reasons and consequences of this phenomenon. We present examples from current common practices of conducting machine learning research (e.g. avoidance of reporting negative results) and failure of generalization ability of the proposed algorithms and datasets in actual real-life usage. Furthermore, a potential future trajectory of machine learning research and development from the perspective of accountable, unbiased, ethical and privacy-aware algorithmic decision making is discussed. We would like to emphasize that with this discussion we neither claim to provide an exhaustive argumentation nor blame any specific institution or individual on the raised issues. This is simply a discussion put forth by us, insiders of the machine learning field, reflecting on us.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of designing effective neural network architectures with minimal human intervention, while ensuring robust generalization across diverse datasets. Prior work has established that automated methods such as reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, and sequential model-based optimization can discover architectures that achieve state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets like CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. However, these approaches often lack rigorous evaluation of their search strategies, and concerns remain about the generalization of models trained on standard test sets. To address these gaps, we develop a method that evaluates the search process itself, rather than only the final performance on downstream tasks. Our approach involves comparing the quality of candidate architectures generated by different search strategies against a baseline of random selection, while also examining the impact of common practices such as weight sharing. We analyze how these factors influence the discovery of effective architectures and assess the reliability of published results in the field. Our evaluation provides insights into the limitations of current search strategies and highlights the need for more transparent and reproducible methods in neural architecture search.

original_abstract: One of the primary challenges faced by deep learning is the degree to which current methods exploit superficial statistics and dataset bias, rather than learning to generalise over the specific representations they have experienced. This is a critical concern because generalisation enables robust reasoning over unseen data, whereas leveraging superficial statistics is fragile to even small changes in data distribution. To illuminate the issue and drive progress towards a solution, we propose a test that explicitly evaluates abstract reasoning over visual data. We introduce a large-scale benchmark of visual questions that involve operations fundamental to many high-level vision tasks, such as comparisons of counts and logical operations on complex visual properties. The benchmark directly measures a method's ability to infer high-level relationships and to generalise them over image-based concepts. It includes multiple training/test splits that require controlled levels of generalization. We evaluate a range of deep learning architectures, and find that existing models, including those popular for vision-and-language tasks, are unable to solve seemingly-simple instances. Models using relational networks fare better but leave substantial room for improvement.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of enabling models to answer questions about visual content with greater flexibility and reasoning capability. Prior work has established that current methods often rely on fixed mappings between visual and textual modalities, which limit their ability to generalize beyond training data or handle complex reasoning tasks. These approaches frequently fail to account for the structural complexity of both images and questions, leading to suboptimal performance on tasks requiring deeper understanding. To address these limitations, we develop a method that leverages structured representations of both visual scenes and linguistic input, enabling more effective joint reasoning across modalities. Our approach constructs graph-based representations that capture relationships within the image and the question, and employs a deep neural network designed to exploit these structures. We evaluate the effectiveness of this method on established benchmarks, demonstrating improvements in accuracy and reasoning capabilities compared to existing approaches. Our results highlight the potential of structured representations in advancing the field of visual question answering.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a Dual Focal Loss (DFL) function, as a replacement for the standard cross entropy (CE) function to achieve a better treatment of the unbalanced classes in a dataset. Our DFL method is an improvement on the recently reported Focal Loss (FL) cross-entropy function, which proposes a scaling method that puts more weight on the examples that are difficult to classify over those that are easy. However, the scaling parameter of FL is empirically set, which is problem-dependent. In addition, like other CE variants, FL only focuses on the loss of true classes. Therefore, no loss feedback is gained from the false classes. Although focusing only on true examples increases probability on true classes and correspondingly reduces probability on false classes due to the nature of the softmax function, it does not achieve the best convergence due to avoidance of the loss on false classes. Our DFL method improves on the simple FL in two ways. Firstly, it takes the idea of FL to focus more on difficult examples than the easy ones, but evaluates loss on both true and negative classes with equal importance. Secondly, the scaling parameter of DFL has been made learnable so that it can tune itself by backpropagation rather than being dependent on manual tuning. In this way, our proposed DFL method offers an auto-tunable loss function that can reduce the class imbalance effect as well as put more focus on both true difficult examples and negative easy examples. Experimental results show that our proposed method provides better accuracy in every test run conducted over a variety of different network models and datasets.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of accurately and efficiently segmenting brain tumors in magnetic resonance images, a task complicated by the irregular shapes, sizes, and locations of such tumors. Prior work has established the effectiveness of deep neural networks, particularly convolutional architectures, in capturing both local and contextual features for segmentation. However, challenges remain in handling class imbalance, improving inference speed, and refining boundary detection. To address these, we develop a novel architecture that integrates multi-scale feature extraction with a refined loss function designed to counteract data imbalance. The model employs an encoder-decoder structure with atrous separable convolutions to capture contextual information and sharp boundaries, while incorporating hierarchical loss mechanisms to improve segmentation accuracy. We also implement a two-phase training strategy to enhance robustness and efficiency. The approach is evaluated on benchmark datasets, demonstrating improvements in segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing methods.

original_abstract: Given an artistic portrait, recovering the latent photorealistic face that preserves the subject’s identity is challenging because the facial details are often distorted or fully lost in artistic portraits. We develop an Identity-preserving Face Recovery from Portraits method that utilizes a Style Removal network (SRN) and a Discriminative Network (DN). Our SRN, composed of an autoencoder with residual block-embedded skip connections, is designed to transfer feature maps of stylized images to the feature maps of the corresponding photorealistic faces. Owing to the Spatial Transformer Network, SRN automatically compensates for misalignments of stylized portraits to output aligned realistic face images. To ensure the identity preservation, we promote the recovered and ground truth faces to share similar visual features via a distance measure which compares features of recovered and ground truth faces extracted from a pre-trained FaceNet network. DN has multiple convolutional and fully-connected layers, and its role is to enforce recovered faces to be similar to authentic faces. Thus, we can recover high-quality photorealistic faces from unaligned portraits while preserving the identity of the face in an image. By conducting extensive evaluations on a large-scale synthesized dataset and a hand-drawn sketch dataset, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior face recovery and attains state-of-the-art results. In addition, our method can recover photorealistic faces from unseen stylized portraits, artistic paintings, and hand-drawn sketches.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-quality, flexible, and efficient image stylization that preserves content integrity while adapting to arbitrary styles. Prior work has established that neural networks can capture and transfer artistic styles through feature statistics, yet existing methods often struggle with balancing speed, quality, diversity, and user control. To address these limitations, we develop a framework that integrates perceptual and statistical constraints into a unified learning process. Our approach employs a feed-forward architecture trained with a combination of perceptual losses and histogram-based objectives, enabling the synthesis of textures and stylized images that better match the statistical properties of exemplars while maintaining content coherence. We also incorporate mechanisms for fine-grained control over style composition and spatial distribution. The method is evaluated on a range of tasks, including texture synthesis, artistic style transfer, and stylized image generation, demonstrating improvements in visual quality, convergence speed, and flexibility compared to prior approaches.

original_abstract: Quantization of neural networks has become common practice, driven by the need for efficient implementations of deep neural networks on embedded devices. In this paper, we exploit an oft-overlooked degree of freedom in most networks - for a given layer, individual output channels can be scaled by any factor provided that the corresponding weights of the next layer are inversely scaled. Therefore, a given network has many factorizations which change the weights of the network without changing its function. We present a conceptually simple and easy to implement method that uses this property and show that proper factorizations significantly decrease the degradation caused by quantization. We show improvement on a wide variety of networks and achieve state-of-the-art degradation results for MobileNets. While our focus is on quantization, this type of factorization is applicable to other domains such as network-pruning, neural nets regularization and network interpretability.
generated_abstract: This work addresses the challenge of deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained hardware by reducing their computational and memory demands through low-precision quantization. Prior research has established that deep networks can be trained and deployed with limited numerical precision, often achieving comparable accuracy to full-precision models through techniques such as stochastic rounding, weight pruning, and quantization-aware training. However, the effectiveness of these methods in maintaining accuracy while minimizing precision remains an open question, particularly when applied to a wide range of architectures and deployment scenarios. To address this, we develop a method that incrementally quantizes network weights while preserving accuracy through a combination of adaptive bit-width allocation, fine-tuning, and careful calibration of activation ranges. Our approach evaluates the impact of these strategies on a variety of deep learning models, focusing on their ability to maintain performance at significantly reduced precision levels. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high accuracy with low-precision weights, enabling efficient deployment on embedded systems.

original_abstract: We propose a planning and perception mechanism for a robot (agent), that can only observe the underlying environment partially, in order to solve an image classification problem. A three-layer architecture is suggested that consists of a meta-layer that decides the intermediate goals, an action-layer that selects local actions as the agent navigates towards a goal, and a classification-layer that evaluates the reward and makes a prediction. We design and implement these layers using deep reinforcement learning. A generalized policy gradient algorithm is utilized to learn the parameters of these layers to maximize the expected reward. Our proposed methodology is tested on the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, which provides us with a level of explainability while interpreting the agent's intermediate goals and course of action.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving the efficiency and accuracy of deep learning models in complex visual recognition tasks. Prior work has established that deeper networks can achieve better performance but are harder to train, and that architectures with dense connectivity or micro networks can enhance feature abstraction and reduce overfitting. However, the integration of these concepts into a unified framework that supports both effective feature learning and efficient training remains an open problem. To address this, we develop a model that combines dense connectivity with micro network structures to enhance local feature learning while maintaining computational efficiency. The mechanism involves stacking layers where each layer receives inputs from all preceding layers and employs micro networks to refine local representations. This approach is evaluated on standard benchmark datasets to assess its effectiveness in improving classification accuracy and reducing model complexity.

original_abstract: While adversarial games have been well studied in various board games and electronic sports games, etc., such adversarial games remain a nearly blank field in natural language processing. As natural language is inherently an interactive game, we propose a challenging pragmatics game called Adversarial Taboo, in which an attacker and a defender compete with each other through sequential natural language interactions. The attacker is tasked with inducing the defender to speak a target word invisible to the defender, while the defender is tasked with detecting the target word before being induced by the attacker. In Adversarial Taboo, a successful attacker must hide its intention and subtly induce the defender, while a competitive defender must be cautious with its utterances and infer the intention of the attacker. To instantiate the game, we create a game environment and a competition platform. Sufficient pilot experiments and empirical studies on several baseline attack and defense strategies show promising and interesting results. Based on the analysis on the game and experiments, we discuss multiple promising directions for future research.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of building dialogue systems that can engage in natural, goal-oriented conversations by integrating multiple aspects of language understanding and generation. Prior work has established methods for generating responses using hierarchical neural models, improving diversity through alternative objective functions, and incorporating pragmatic reasoning and reinforcement learning to guide dialogue flow. However, open questions remain regarding how to effectively combine these elements into a unified framework that supports both flexible interaction and strategic communication. To address this, we develop a model that integrates hierarchical sequence generation with reinforcement learning and pragmatic reasoning, enabling agents to plan ahead and adapt their responses based on inferred intentions and contextual goals. The model is trained on a diverse set of dialogue scenarios, including negotiation and collaborative tasks, and is evaluated on its ability to produce coherent, goal-aligned responses that reflect both linguistic fluency and strategic reasoning.

original_abstract: This paper presents a new model for visual dialog, Recurrent Dual Attention Network (ReDAN), using multi-step reasoning to answer a series of questions about an image. In each question-answering turn of a dialog, ReDAN infers the answer progressively through multiple reasoning steps. In each step of the reasoning process, the semantic representation of the question is updated based on the image and the previous dialog history, and the recurrently-refined representation is used for further reasoning in the subsequent step. On the VisDial v1.0 dataset, the proposed ReDAN model achieves a new state-of-the-art of 64.47% NDCG score. Visualization on the reasoning process further demonstrates that ReDAN can locate context-relevant visual and textual clues via iterative refinement, which can lead to the correct answer step-by-step.
generated_abstract: Visual dialog requires an agent to answer a sequence of interdependent questions about an image while maintaining contextual coherence. Prior work has established the importance of attention mechanisms in resolving visual references and integrating dialog history, as well as the value of incorporating answers into the reasoning process. However, challenges remain in effectively modeling the interplay between image content, question context, and answer relevance across multiple turns. This work introduces a novel framework that combines multi-stage reasoning with dynamic attention mechanisms to better align visual and linguistic information throughout the dialog. The approach first identifies relevant image regions using a hierarchical attention process, then integrates historical context and question dependencies through a dual-path network. Finally, it refines candidate answers by synergizing image-question relevance with answer-based feedback. The method is evaluated on standard visual dialog benchmarks, demonstrating improvements in both discriminative and generative tasks.

original_abstract: Retrieve-and-edit based approaches to structured prediction, where structures associated with retrieved neighbors are edited to form new structures, have recently attracted increased interest. However, much recent work merely conditions on retrieved structures (e.g., in a sequence-to-sequence framework), rather than explicitly manipulating them. We show we can perform accurate sequence labeling by explicitly (and only) copying labels from retrieved neighbors. Moreover, because this copying is label-agnostic, we can achieve impressive performance in zero-shot sequence-labeling tasks. We additionally consider a dynamic programming approach to sequence labeling in the presence of retrieved neighbors, which allows for controlling the number of distinct (copied) segments used to form a prediction, and leads to both more interpretable and accurate predictions.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving sequence labeling performance in low-resource and cross-lingual settings by leveraging pre-trained contextual representations and transfer learning. Prior work has established that end-to-end models combining bidirectional LSTMs, CNNs, and CRFs achieve strong results on standard sequence labeling tasks, while pre-trained deep bidirectional language models provide rich contextualized word representations that enhance performance across multiple NLP tasks. However, the effectiveness of these approaches in scenarios with limited labeled data or across languages remains an open question. To address this, we develop a model that integrates pre-trained contextual representations with hierarchical recurrent networks, enabling knowledge transfer from resource-rich to resource-poor domains. The model is trained using a combination of task-specific and domain-agnostic signals, allowing it to adapt to new tasks with minimal supervision. We evaluate the approach on a range of sequence labeling tasks, demonstrating improvements in performance across both low-resource and cross-lingual settings.

original_abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of how and why face recognition accuracy differs between men and women. We show that accuracy is lower for women due to the combination of (1) the impostor distribution for women having a skew toward higher similarity scores, and (2) the genuine distribution for women having a skew toward lower similarity scores. We show that this phenomenon of the impostor and genuine distributions for women shifting closer towards each other is general across datasets of African-American, Caucasian, and Asian faces. We show that the distribution of facial expressions may differ between male/female, but that the accuracy difference persists for image subsets rated confidently as neutral expression. The accuracy difference also persists for image subsets rated as close to zero pitch angle. Even when removing images with forehead partially occluded by hair/hat, the same impostor/genuine accuracy difference persists. We show that the female genuine distribution improves when only female images without facial cosmetics are used, but that the female impostor distribution also degrades at the same time. Lastly, we show that the accuracy difference persists even if a state-of-the-art deep learning method is trained from scratch using training data explicitly balanced between male and female images and subjects.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving face recognition accuracy under varying conditions such as age, pose, and illumination, where existing methods often struggle to maintain consistent performance. Prior work has established that deep learning models, when trained with specialized loss functions such as angular softmax or cosine margin losses, can produce more discriminative features by enforcing geometric constraints in a hypersphere manifold. However, the impact of covariates on model performance and the effectiveness of training strategies to mitigate these effects remain underexplored. To address this, we develop a method that incorporates covariate-aware training strategies to enhance model robustness. Our approach leverages large-scale datasets with diverse covariates to refine feature learning, ensuring that the model adapts to variations in age, pose, and other factors. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating improvements in recognition accuracy across different demographic groups and challenging conditions.

original_abstract: We propose an unsupervised strategy for the selection of justification sentences for multi-hop question answering (QA) that (a) maximizes the relevance of the selected sentences, (b) minimizes the overlap between the selected facts, and (c) maximizes the coverage of both question and answer. This unsupervised sentence selection method can be coupled with any supervised QA approach. We show that the sentences selected by our method improve the performance of a state-of-the-art supervised QA model on two multi-hop QA datasets: AI2's Reasoning Challenge (ARC) and Multi-Sentence Reading Comprehension (MultiRC). We obtain new state-of-the-art performance on both datasets among approaches that do not use external resources for training the QA system: 56.82\% F1 on ARC (41.24\% on Challenge and 64.49\% on Easy) and 26.1\% EM0 on MultiRC. Our justification sentences have higher quality than the justifications selected by a strong information retrieval baseline, e.g., by 5.4\% F1 in MultiRC. We also show that our unsupervised selection of justification sentences is more stable across domains than a state-of-the-art supervised sentence selection method.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of answering complex questions that require reasoning across multiple documents or passages, where answers are not directly stated but must be inferred from distributed evidence. Prior work has established methods for single-document question answering and initial approaches for multi-hop reasoning, yet significant gaps remain in effectively aggregating and verifying evidence from multiple sources. To address these gaps, we develop a model that integrates information across passages through a structured verification process, enabling the system to evaluate and reconcile conflicting or complementary evidence. Our approach employs a neural architecture that jointly considers answer boundaries, content, and cross-passage consistency to refine candidate answers. We evaluate this method on established multi-passage and multi-hop question answering datasets, demonstrating improvements in accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods. The results highlight the effectiveness of cross-passage verification in enhancing the reliability of answers derived from distributed information.
